But that idea calls for another one. If code is a system, then it is not enough for it to be pleasant to write, locally fluid to read, or elegant in appearance. Its structures must remain visible. Its boundaries, states, contracts, responsibilities, and effects must be understandable, revisitable, criticizable, and transformable. In other words: the system must be explicit. This is where a very contemporary tension appears. For a long time, part of software tooling has valued the implicit: conventions, framework magic, inferred behaviors, invisible structures, shortcuts that let us move faster. This has often been useful. It has sometimes even been very productive. But in the age of intelligences — human and artificial — the implicit changes in nature. xl4d5i:310: —In the era of humans and AI agents co-programming code, implicit conventions are undergoing a fundamental change in nature. The article's central argument: implicitness has never been merely about being "hidden" — its essence is reliance on shared assumptions. Framework magic, convention inference, filename routing — these work in traditional software development because the collaborating humans always share the same context: they work in the same IDE, follow the same code review process, and read the same internal documentation. When AI agents join the collaboration chain, that shared assumption breaks. An agent does not "inherit" the developers' tacit understanding; it never experienced the same accumulation of technical debt, nor participated in decisions discussed without documentation. So to an agent, implicit structures are not "conventional wisdom" but opaque obstacles.
xn5n97:256: —The article is not calling for the complete elimination of implicit design, but rather for a more refined framework of judgment. The author acknowledges that implicitness is an "accelerator" that has historically driven productivity gains in tools and frameworks. The key question is not "should we use implicitness" but "who needs to understand this implicitness." In a purely human team, implicitness can be shared only among the same team members and does not need to be globally visible. But when Agents participate in collaboration, all collaborating Agents must be able to "understand" these implicit patterns — and under current technical conditions, this requires them to be explicit. This means that when organizations introduce AI coding tools, they need to conduct a systematic "Agent-understandability" review of existing framework implicit patterns.
